show_notes:
**[Recommendations for the use of hormone and nonhormone treatment of vasomotor symptoms of menopause: Menopause Medical Eligibility Criteria (MenoMEC) based on insights from a modified Delphi panel](https://doi.org/10.1097/GME.0000000000002947)**

*Menopause, 2026*

DOI: [10.1097/GME.0000000000002947](https://doi.org/10.1097/GME.0000000000002947)

**Question:** Can a US expert panel agree which hormone and nonhormone treatments for menopausal hot flashes suit women with specific comorbidities?

**Answer:** A 15-physician modified Delphi (11 answered the survey; consensus at ≥70% agreement) built a 1–4 eligibility grid. Every comorbidity item failed online consensus and was settled in person, with no vote tallies reported.

**Three takeaways**

1. Measured agreement covers the uncontroversial: hormone therapy first-line when safe, clonidine unanimously rejected, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, oxybutynin and NK-targeted drugs as alternatives.
2. All comorbidity questions missed the 70% bar online; their resolution in person is expert judgment of unreported unanimity.
3. The contraceptive-style grid separates initiation from continuation and relative from absolute risk, so prior VTE is no longer an automatic no.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo. This is the Friday pick. The science subreddit didn't turn up anything usable this week, so we went to the most-discussed papers on PubMed instead, and this one was sitting at the top.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's in Menopause, from Jill Liss and colleagues: recommendations for treating hot flashes and night sweats, with and without hormones, built from a modified Delphi panel. The product is a grid. Which drug, for which woman, given whatever else she has going on.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So it's a guideline, not an experiment. There's no new data in a consensus statement, by design. Why is that worth ten minutes?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Because the method is the paper. A Delphi is how medicine manufactures agreement when the trials don't exist, and this one lets you look at the machinery. And the format they chose is genuinely clever.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Quick setup. Vasomotor symptoms, the clinical term for hot flashes and night sweats, are among the most common and disruptive parts of the menopause transition. The standard treatment is hormone therapy: estrogen, plus a progestogen if the woman still has a uterus. But plenty of women can't take it or won't. A past breast cancer, a past blood clot, heart disease. For them, the authors argue, the guidance on alternatives is thin and inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the alternatives are what, exactly?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mostly borrowed drugs, used off-label. The S-S-R-I and S-N-R-I antidepressants, gabapentin, which is an anticonvulsant, and oxybutynin, a bladder drug. Then a more recently approved class, the neurokinin-targeted drugs, fezolinetant and elinzanetant.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Now remind me how a Delphi panel actually works, because I suspect this whole episode hangs on the mechanics.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Classically, experts rate statements anonymously, see the group's aggregate, and rate again, over several rounds. In the authors' own description, anonymity lets every view carry equal weight, without the pressures of open debate. Theirs is modified: one anonymous online survey, then an in-person meeting where items that hadn't reached agreement were discussed and re-voted. Fifteen physicians, each statement rated on a nine-point scale, and an item counted as consensus if seventy percent of panelists landed in the same band, seven to nine for agreement, one to three for disagreement.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm. Credit for that before I complain about anything. They wrote the bar down in advance. In episode eighty-seven, the essay on whether the twenty twenty-four election was a mandate, nobody said what result would count, so the verdict couldn't come out the other way. Here the threshold was on paper before anyone voted.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is. So here's the central claim as I'd state it: a multidisciplinary American panel reached consensus on which treatments suit which women, and encoded that consensus in a one-to-four eligibility grid. The question is how much of the grid that bar actually covers.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right. So how many of the fifteen answered the anonymous survey?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Eleven of the fifteen.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh, so the bar was really seventy percent of eleven. That's eight people, in the one round that's actually anonymous.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yes. And, well, the more important part is what failed. Online, the panel did not reach agreement on choosing hormone or non-hormone therapy for women with cardiovascular disease, thrombosis, smoking, metabolic syndrome, hormone-sensitive and non-hormone-sensitive cancers, or liver disease.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Wait. That's every comorbidity. That's the grid.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's most of what makes the grid new, yes. In the authors' words, all of those were discussed and resolved during the consensus meeting.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then there are two readings. In one, the room genuinely converged: people heard the cardiologist and the oncologist reason it through and moved, which is what the modification is for. In the other, the anonymity the authors themselves call the point of a Delphi disappeared precisely where it was needed. Those two produce identical grids. So what does the paper report from the re-vote?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Um, so, nothing quantitative. The methods say items were discussed and re-voted. The results don't give a tally for any of them. No count of how many items passed online, none for how many passed in the room, and no vote split on any comorbidity cell.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right, so the rule I just praised is never shown being applied to the decisions that matter.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's fair. And the first meeting, in March twenty twenty-five, had all fifteen. The final one, a year later, to finalise the recommendations, had ten. Seven in the room, three online.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: I'm not saying the answer is wrong. But the authors list participation that varied slightly as a limitation, and a third of the panel absent from the final meeting isn't what I'd call slight.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Let me be fair to the output, then. Where the grid is definite, what does it say?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hormone therapy is first-line for moderate to severe symptoms in women without contraindications. For non-hormone options, the antidepressants, gabapentin and oxybutynin, with the neurokinin drugs supported as first-line where cost and access allow. Clonidine, a blood pressure drug, was unanimously not recommended, for lack of efficacy and a risk of low blood pressure.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm-hm. Unanimous on clonidine is clean. It's also, I'd guess, the item nobody needed a panel for.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Probably. What I'd credit is the format. They modelled it on the American Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, a grid American clinicians already know. Category one, no restriction. Two, advantages generally outweigh the risks. Three, risks usually outweigh the advantages. Four, unacceptable risk, don't use it. And each therapy gets separate ratings for starting it and for continuing it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Ah, okay, that starting-versus-continuing split is the interesting move. Those are different decisions, and a flat list of contraindications collapses them.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Age shows it best. Over seventy, they judge the risks of hormone therapy generally greater than the benefits. In the sixties, continuing a transdermal patch generally favours the advantages, while starting oral hormones generally doesn't.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. So the same woman gets a different answer depending on whether she's already on it, and by which route. That's more useful than yes or no.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And the line between three and four does real work on blood clots. Early on, a prior venous clot is listed among the contraindications to hormone therapy. Later, the panel says a prior clot should not be treated as a uniform contraindication. Oral estrogen should usually be avoided afterwards, but low-dose transdermal estradiol may be reasonable, particularly after a clearly provoked event, one following surgery, say.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hold on. Those two statements are in the same paper. Which one is the grid?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hmm. The later one, I think. They say the split between three and four exists precisely to separate relative from absolute contraindications, and that clots and cardiovascular events can be relative in some scenarios. But the earlier sentence is still there, unqualified. And the support they cite for the transdermal route after a clot is, in their own words, limited observational data.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is the shape of the whole thing. The panel isn't generating evidence, it's deciding how to act on thin evidence, which is a legitimate job. But every hard cell is a judgment, and the reader can't see how divided it was. Who was actually in the room?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Gynecology, menopause specialists, oncology, cardiology, endocrinology, neurology, bone health, hematology and psychiatry. All of them received an honorarium, which the paper discloses. The text we have doesn't say who funded the process.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Then I notice what's missing from that list. The grid is pitched at primary care, which is where they say most of this management happens. The specialties they name don't include family medicine or general internal medicine. And it was all physicians, no patients. The people who'll use the grid weren't voting, and neither were the people it's used on.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Well, that's accurate as far as the paper describes the panel. In fairness, they chose it for expertise in menopause and in the comorbidities, which is what you'd want for the hard cells.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Yeah. There's a quieter version of the same issue, though. Who wrote the questions?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The survey items came out of their own systematic review of American guidelines, and a first draft was refined with feedback from two of the authors. Forty-one questions on treatment, plus a handful on diagnosis and unmet need.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's episode ninety-one's problem, the interviews with young men about sex, where the guide never asked how sex feels and the absence of enjoyment became the headline. A Delphi panel can only agree or disagree with statements someone put in front of it. Nothing the drafters didn't phrase can reach consensus. Nobody has to steer. The instrument sets the space of possible answers.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: One more place to separate claim from data. On the neurokinin drugs, panelists noted that clinicians want them for their fast onset, working within one week with minimal side effects, but that insurers often demand a four- to six-week trial of an off-label drug first.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Uh, within a week and minimal side effects. Where does that come from?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's from the discussion, not from data in this paper. And the same paper says these drugs need routine liver function monitoring, that fezolinetant is contraindicated in cirrhosis, and that elinzanetant may cause sleepiness. The authors also name limited long-term safety data on this class as a gap.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So minimal side effects sits next to mandatory liver tests. I'd want the trial numbers for that claim, not the room's impression of them.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Credit where it's due, though. Their limitations are plain: the consensus reflects expert opinion rather than direct empirical evidence, and the recommendations may need prospective validation. And they close by calling the grid a decision-support framework rather than a prescriptive guideline.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Though the abstract calls it a guideline, and that's the word that travels. So, a verdict. As evidence, it adds nothing, and says so. As a format, it's the American counterpart to the hormone therapy eligibility criteria a consortium of Spanish societies published in twenty twenty-two, and its one genuinely good idea is borrowing the contraceptive grid. Whether it's a consensus in the sense its own methods define, the paper doesn't let you check.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah, I'd sign that, with one softening. Even if you treat every hard cell as one group's opinion, the grid is still more usable than a list of contraindications.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Agreed. Three takeaways. One: what the panel measurably agreed on is the uncontroversial part. Hormone therapy first when it's safe, clonidine out, antidepressants, gabapentin, oxybutynin and the neurokinin drugs as alternatives.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Two: every comorbidity question failed the seventy percent bar online and was settled in a room, with no tallies reported, so the hard cells are expert judgment of unknown unanimity. Three: the useful idea is the format, a one-to-four grid that separates starting from continuing, and relative from absolute risk, so a past clot stops being an automatic no.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: What would change my mind is the re-vote, item by item. If the comorbidity cells cleared seventy percent by anonymous ballot, most of this objection goes away.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: For me it's use: primary care clinicians given cases with and without the grid, scored against an independent panel. Until then I'd believe this is a sensible summary of what these fifteen people think. I wouldn't yet call it the field's consensus.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's Liss and colleagues, in Menopause, twenty twenty-six.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Thanks for listening.
